sections.title: Section A — common to Mathematics and Applied Mathematics (compulsory)

questions.topic: Algebra: Matrices, Determinants, Inverse and the Matrix Method
questions.sub_topic: Determinant of the inverse of a diagonal matrix
questions.question: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&2&0\\0&0&3\end{bmatrix}\), then \(|A^{-1}|\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{1}{6}\)
Given: \(|A| = 1 \times 2 \times 3 = 6\)
Formula: \(|A^{-1}| = \dfrac{1}{|A|}\)
Step 1: \(|A^{-1}| = \dfrac{1}{6}\)
Common mistake: \(6\) (A) is \(|A|\) itself. \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) (B) uses only the last diagonal entry.
Key point: The determinant of a diagonal matrix is the product of its diagonal entries.

questions.sub_topic: Order and degree of a first-order linear equation
questions.question: The order and degree of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 3y = x^2\) are:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) order 1, degree 1
Given: only \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) appears, to the power 1
Step 1: Order \(= 1\)
Step 2: Degree \(= 1\)
Common mistake: (B) takes the power of \(x^2\) as the degree. (A) counts the terms.
Key point: Powers of \(x\) do not affect the degree.

questions.topic: Algebra: Matrices, Determinants, Inverse and the Matrix Method
questions.sub_topic: Value of A² − 2A for a 2 × 2 matrix
questions.question: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix}3&1\\2&-1\end{bmatrix}\), then \(A^2 - 2A\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(5I\)
Given: \(A = \begin{bmatrix}3&1\\2&-1\end{bmatrix}\)
Formula: \(A^2 = A \cdot A\), then subtract \(2A\)
Step 1: \(A^2 = \begin{bmatrix}9 + 2&3 - 1\\6 - 2&2 + 1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}11&2\\4&3\end{bmatrix}\)
Step 2: \(2A = \begin{bmatrix}6&2\\4&-2\end{bmatrix}\)
Step 3: \(A^2 - 2A = \begin{bmatrix}5&0\\0&5\end{bmatrix} = 5I\)
Common mistake: (B) stops at \(A^2\). (C) takes the last entry of \(2A\) as \(+2\), giving \(3 - 2 = 1\).
Key point: Subtracting a negative entry adds it.

questions.topic: Algebra: Matrices, Determinants, Inverse and the Matrix Method
questions.sub_topic: One unknown of a 3 × 3 system
questions.question: For the system \(x + y + z = 3\), \(2x - y + z = 2\), \(x + 2y - z = 2\), the value of \(x\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(1\)
Given: \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1&1&1\\2&-1&1\\1&2&-1\end{bmatrix}\)
Formula: \(x = \dfrac{|A_x|}{|A|}\), where \(A_x\) has the first column replaced by the constants
Step 1: \(|A| = 1(1 - 2) - 1(-2 - 1) + 1(4 + 1) = -1 + 3 + 5 = 7\)
Step 2: \(|A_x| = \begin{vmatrix}3&1&1\\2&-1&1\\2&2&-1\end{vmatrix} = 3(1 - 2) - 1(-2 - 2) + 1(4 + 2) = -3 + 4 + 6 = 7\)
Step 3: \(x = \dfrac{7}{7} = 1\); check: \((1, 1, 1)\) satisfies all three equations ✓
Common mistake: \(-1\) (C) takes the first cofactor of \(|A|\) as \(+1\). \(0\) (B) forgets the third term of \(|A_x|\).
Key point: Check the solution in every equation.

questions.topic: Algebra: Matrices, Determinants, Inverse and the Matrix Method
questions.sub_topic: Transpose of a product
questions.question: For matrices \(A\) and \(B\) for which \(AB\) is defined, \((AB)^T\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(B^TA^T\)
Why: The transpose of a product is the product of the transposes in reverse order: \((AB)^T = B^TA^T\).
Why not the others: (A) keeps the original order, which may not even be defined. (C) and (D) ignore the transpose.
Key point: Reverse the order, as with inverses: \((AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}\).

questions.sub_topic: An objective parallel to a boundary edge
questions.question:
For \(Z = x + 2y\) subject to \(x + 2y \le 8\), \(x, y \ge 0\), consider the following statements:
(A) The feasible region is a triangle.
(B) Its corner points are \((0, 0)\), \((8, 0)\) and \((0, 4)\).
(C) The maximum value of \(Z\) is 8.
(D) The maximum of \(Z\) occurs at exactly one point.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D) only
Why: \(Z\) is 8 at both \((8, 0)\) and \((0, 4)\). Only (D) is false: every point of the segment joining them also gives \(Z = 8\).
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) agree with the region and the corner values. Options (A), (B) and (C) name a true statement as false.
Key point: When the objective is parallel to an edge, the whole edge can be optimal.

questions.sub_topic: Separable equation (x + 1)/(y − 1)
questions.question: The general solution of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x + 1}{y - 1}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(y^2 - 2y = x^2 + 2x + C\)
Given: \((y - 1)\,dy = (x + 1)\,dx\)
Formula: integrate both sides
Step 1: \(\dfrac{y^2}{2} - y = \dfrac{x^2}{2} + x + c\)
Step 2: Multiply by 2: \(y^2 - 2y = x^2 + 2x + C\)
Common mistake: (B) changes the sign of the \(y\) term. (C) does not integrate.
Key point: After separating, integrate each side term by term.

questions.topic: Calculus: Derivatives, Increasing/Decreasing Functions, Maxima and Minima
questions.sub_topic: Second derivative of log x
questions.question: If \(y = \log x\) (\(x > 0\)), then \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(-\dfrac{1}{x^2}\)
Given: \(y = \log x\)
Formula: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}x^{-1} = -x^{-2}\)
Step 1: \(y' = \dfrac{1}{x}\)
Step 2: \(y'' = -\dfrac{1}{x^2}\)
Common mistake: (A) is the first derivative. (C) loses the minus sign.
Key point: Write \(\dfrac{1}{x}\) as \(x^{-1}\) before differentiating.

questions.topic: Calculus: Derivatives, Increasing/Decreasing Functions, Maxima and Minima
questions.sub_topic: A cubic that is always increasing
questions.question:
For \(f(x) = x^3 + 3x\), consider the following statements:
(A) \(f'(x) > 0\) for every real \(x\).
(B) \(f\) is strictly increasing on \(\mathbb{R}\).
(C) \(f\) has no local maximum or minimum.
(D) \(f\) has a local minimum at \(x = 0\).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) \(f'(x) = 3x^2 + 3 \ge 3 > 0\). (B) follows from (A). (C) \(f'\) is never zero, so there are no critical points.
Why not the others: (D) is false: \(f'(0) = 3 \ne 0\). Options (C) and (D) include (D); (B) leaves out (C).
Key point: Extrema need \(f'\) to change sign; here it is always positive.

questions.sub_topic: Four basic definite integrals
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) \(\int_0^1 x\,dx\)
(B) \(\int_0^1 x^2\,dx\)
(C) \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos x\,dx\)
(D) \(\int_0^1 e^x\,dx\)

List-II
(I) \(1\)
(II) \(\dfrac{1}{2}\)
(III) \(e - 1\)
(IV) \(\dfrac{1}{3}\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Step 1: \(\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^1 = \dfrac{1}{2}\) (II)
Step 2: \(\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = \dfrac{1}{3}\) (IV)
Step 3: \([\sin x]_0^{\pi/2} = 1\) (I)
Step 4: \([e^x]_0^1 = e - 1\) (III)
Common mistake: (A) swaps the first two. (C) swaps \(\int x^2\) and \(\int \cos x\). (D) forgets \(e^0 = 1\) and swaps the last two.
Key point: Always subtract the value at the lower limit.

questions.sub_topic: Mean number of sixes in two throws
questions.question: A die is thrown twice. If \(X\) is the number of sixes obtained, then \(E(X)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{1}{3}\)
Given: \(X = 0, 1, 2\)
Formula: \(E(X) = \sum xP(X = x)\)
Step 1: \(P(0) = \dfrac{25}{36}\), \(P(1) = 2 \times \dfrac{1}{6} \times \dfrac{5}{6} = \dfrac{10}{36}\), \(P(2) = \dfrac{1}{36}\)
Step 2: \(E(X) = \dfrac{10}{36} + \dfrac{2}{36} = \dfrac{12}{36} = \dfrac{1}{3}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{11}{36}\) (B) is \(P(X \ge 1)\). \(\dfrac{1}{6}\) (A) is the chance of a six on one throw.
Key point: The mean counts two sixes twice.

questions.sub_topic: Integral of 1 + tan² x
questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int (1 + \tan^2 x)\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\tan x + C\)
Given: \(1 + \tan^2 x = \sec^2 x\)
Formula: \(\int \sec^2 x\,dx = \tan x + C\)
Step 1: \(\int \sec^2 x\,dx = \tan x + C\)
Common mistake: (B) treats \(\tan x\) as if it were \(x\). (D) integrates the 1 separately but then integrates \(\tan^2 x\) as \(\tan x\).
Key point: Use the identity before integrating.

questions.topic: Calculus: Derivatives, Increasing/Decreasing Functions, Maxima and Minima
questions.sub_topic: Nearest point of a parabola to a point on its axis
questions.question: The shortest distance from the point \((0, 1.5)\) to the curve \(y = x^2\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\)
Given: a point on the curve is \((x, x^2)\)
Formula: minimise \(D = d^2 = x^2 + (x^2 - 1.5)^2\); put \(t = x^2 \ge 0\)
Step 1: \(D(t) = t + (t - 1.5)^2\); \(D'(t) = 1 + 2(t - 1.5) = 0 \Rightarrow t = 1\)
Step 2: \(D(1) = 1 + 0.25 = 1.25\) (less than \(D(0) = 2.25\))
Step 3: Shortest distance \(= \sqrt{1.25} = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\)
Common mistake: \(1.5\) (A) is the distance to the vertex \((0, 0)\), which is not the nearest point.
Key point: Minimise the square of the distance; it has the same minimising point.

questions.sub_topic: Fifty-three Sundays in a leap year
questions.question: The probability that a leap year chosen at random has 53 Sundays is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\dfrac{2}{7}\)
Given: 366 days \(= 52\) weeks \(+ 2\) days
Formula: the 2 extra days form one of 7 equally likely pairs
Step 1: Pairs: (Sun, Mon), (Mon, Tue), …, (Sat, Sun)
Step 2: Pairs containing Sunday: (Sat, Sun) and (Sun, Mon), so \(P = \dfrac{2}{7}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{1}{7}\) (A) is the answer for an ordinary year, which has one extra day.
Key point: A leap year has two extra days, not one.

questions.sub_topic: Definite integral of 1/(x + 2)
questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int_0^2 \dfrac{dx}{x + 2}\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\log 2\)
Given: limits 0 and 2
Formula: \(\int \dfrac{dx}{x + a} = \log|x + a|\)
Step 1: \([\log(x + 2)]_0^2 = \log 4 - \log 2\)
Step 2: \(= \log\dfrac{4}{2} = \log 2\)
Common mistake: \(\log 4\) (A) forgets the lower limit.
Key point: \(\log a - \log b = \log\dfrac{a}{b}\).

questions.sub_topic: Monotonicity and extrema of 2x³ − 3x²
questions.question:
For \(f(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2\), consider the following statements:
(A) \(f\) is increasing on \((-\infty, 0)\).
(B) \(f\) is decreasing on \((0, 1)\).
(C) The local maximum value of \(f\) is 1.
(D) The local minimum value of \(f\) is \(-1\).
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: \(f'(x) = 6x(x - 1)\). Only (C) is false: the local maximum is at \(x = 0\), with value \(f(0) = 0\).
Why not the others: (A) \(f' > 0\) for \(x < 0\). (B) \(f' < 0\) for \(0 < x < 1\). (D) \(f(1) = 2 - 3 = -1\). Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: The extreme value is \(f\) at the critical point, not the critical point itself.

questions.sub_topic: The integrating-factor method
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) For \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q\), the integrating factor is \(e^{\int P\,dx}\).
(B) For \(\dfrac{dx}{dy} + P_1x = Q_1\), the integrating factor is \(e^{\int P_1\,dy}\).
(C) The integrating factor of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} - y = 1\) is \(e^{-x}\).
(D) Every first-order differential equation is linear.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) and (B) are the two forms of the method. (C) \(P = -1\), so I.F. \(= e^{-x}\).
Why not the others: (D) is false: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = y^2\) is first order but not linear. Options (C) and (D) include (D); (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: The independent variable in the I.F. is the one you integrate with respect to.

questions.sub_topic: A line through a point parallel to a vector
questions.question:
For the line through \((2, -1, 3)\) parallel to \(2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\), consider the following statements:
(A) Its Cartesian equation is \(\dfrac{x - 2}{2} = \dfrac{y + 1}{-1} = \dfrac{z - 3}{2}\).
(B) Its direction cosines are \(\dfrac{2}{3}, -\dfrac{1}{3}, \dfrac{2}{3}\).
(C) It passes through \((4, -2, 5)\).
(D) It passes through the origin.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D) only
Why: Only (D) is false: \((0, 0, 0)\) gives \(\dfrac{-2}{2} = -1\) but \(\dfrac{1}{-1} = -1\) and \(\dfrac{-3}{2} \ne -1\).
Why not the others: (A) uses the point and the direction directly. (B) the magnitude is 3. (C) \(\lambda = 1\) gives \((4, -2, 5)\). Options (A), (B) and (C) name a true statement as false.
Key point: A point lies on the line only if all three ratios are equal.

questions.sub_topic: Bayes' theorem with a double-headed coin
questions.question: A box has three coins: two fair and one double-headed. A coin is picked at random and tossed, and it shows heads. The probability that it is the double-headed coin is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{1}{2}\)
Given: \(P(D) = \dfrac{1}{3}\), \(P(F) = \dfrac{2}{3}\); \(P(H \mid D) = 1\), \(P(H \mid F) = \dfrac{1}{2}\)
Formula: \(P(D \mid H) = \dfrac{P(D)P(H \mid D)}{P(D)P(H \mid D) + P(F)P(H \mid F)}\)
Step 1: Numerator \(= \dfrac{1}{3}\)
Step 2: Denominator \(= \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{2}{3}\)
Step 3: \(P(D \mid H) = \dfrac{1/3}{2/3} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) (A) ignores the evidence of the head. \(\dfrac{2}{3}\) (B) is \(P(H)\).
Key point: Seeing heads makes the double-headed coin more likely than before.

questions.sub_topic: Unknown in a symmetric matrix
questions.question: If \(\begin{bmatrix}2&x + 1\\3&4\end{bmatrix}\) is symmetric, then \(x\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(2\)
Given: symmetric means \(a_{12} = a_{21}\)
Step 1: \(x + 1 = 3 \Rightarrow x = 2\)
Common mistake: \(3\) (A) sets \(x = 3\) without subtracting 1. \(-2\) (D) solves \(x + 1 = -1\), a sign slip.
Key point: Mirror entries across the diagonal are equal.

questions.sub_topic: Definite integral of cos² x on [0, π/2]
questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^2 x\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\)
Given: \(\cos^2 x = \dfrac{1 + \cos 2x}{2}\)
Formula: \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos 2x\,dx = \left[\dfrac{\sin 2x}{2}\right]_0^{\pi/2} = 0\)
Step 1: \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{1}{2}dx = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\)
Step 2: Total \(= \dfrac{\pi}{4} + 0 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) (A) forgets the \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) in the identity.
Key point: Over \([0, \pi/2]\), \(\cos^2 x\) and \(\sin^2 x\) have the same integral, \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

questions.sub_topic: A sliding ladder
questions.question: A 5 m ladder leans against a vertical wall. Its foot slides away from the wall at 2 m/s. When the foot is 4 m from the wall, the top slides down the wall at:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\dfrac{8}{3}\) m/s
Given: \(x^2 + y^2 = 25\), \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 2\), \(x = 4\) so \(y = 3\)
Formula: differentiate with respect to \(t\)
Step 1: \(2x\dfrac{dx}{dt} + 2y\dfrac{dy}{dt} = 0\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = -\dfrac{x}{y}\dfrac{dx}{dt} = -\dfrac{4}{3} \times 2 = -\dfrac{8}{3}\)
Step 3: The top slides down at \(\dfrac{8}{3}\) m/s
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{3}{2}\) (B) uses \(\dfrac{y}{x}\) instead of \(\dfrac{x}{y}\). \(2\) (C) assumes both ends move at the same speed.
Key point: The ladder's length is fixed, so the two rates are linked.

questions.sub_topic: Integral of cos x/(1 + sin x)
questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{\cos x}{1 + \sin x}\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\log|1 + \sin x| + C\)
Given: the numerator is the derivative of \(1 + \sin x\)
Formula: \(\int \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}dx = \log|f(x)| + C\)
Step 1: \(\log|1 + \sin x| + C\)
Common mistake: (D) adds a minus sign, as for \(\int \tan x\,dx\). (C) uses the \(\tan^{-1}\) form, which needs \(1 + \sin^2 x\).
Key point: Look for the derivative of the denominator in the numerator.

questions.topic: Unit III: Applications of the Integrals
questions.sub_topic: Four standard areas
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Region)
(A) Under \(y = x\) from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 3\), above the \(x\)-axis
(B) Inside the circle \(x^2 + y^2 = 16\)
(C) Under \(y = 2\) from \(x = 1\) to \(x = 4\), above the \(x\)-axis
(D) Inside the ellipse \(\dfrac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 1\)

List-II (Area in sq units)
(I) \(6\)
(II) \(2\pi\)
(III) \(\dfrac{9}{2}\)
(IV) \(16\pi\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Step 1: \(\int_0^3 x\,dx = \dfrac{9}{2}\) (III)
Step 2: \(\pi r^2 = 16\pi\) (IV)
Step 3: \(\int_1^4 2\,dx = 6\) (I)
Step 4: \(\pi ab = \pi(2)(1) = 2\pi\) (II)
Common mistake: (B) swaps the triangle and the circle. (C) swaps the circle and the rectangle. (D) swaps the rectangle and the ellipse.
Key point: Check simple regions with geometry: triangle, rectangle, \(\pi r^2\), \(\pi ab\).

questions.sub_topic: Area of a parallelogram from its diagonals
questions.question: The diagonals of a parallelogram are \(3\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}\) and \(\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\). Its area is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(5\sqrt{3}\) sq units
Given: \(\vec{d}_1 = (3, 1, -2)\), \(\vec{d}_2 = (1, -3, 4)\)
Formula: Area \(= \dfrac{1}{2}|\vec{d}_1 \times \vec{d}_2|\)
Step 1: \(\vec{d}_1 \times \vec{d}_2 = \begin{vmatrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\3&1&-2\\1&-3&4\end{vmatrix} = (4 - 6)\hat{i} - (12 + 2)\hat{j} + (-9 - 1)\hat{k} = -2\hat{i} - 14\hat{j} - 10\hat{k}\)
Step 2: Magnitude \(= \sqrt{4 + 196 + 100} = \sqrt{300} = 10\sqrt{3}\)
Step 3: Area \(= 5\sqrt{3}\)
Common mistake: \(10\sqrt{3}\) (A) forgets the \(\dfrac{1}{2}\), which applies when diagonals (not sides) are given.
Key point: Sides: \(|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|\). Diagonals: \(\dfrac{1}{2}|\vec{d}_1 \times \vec{d}_2|\).

questions.sub_topic: Sum of three principal values
questions.question: The value of \(\tan^{-1}1 + \cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + \sin^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\)
Given: principal branches
Step 1: \(\tan^{-1}1 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\)
Step 2: \(\cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\); \(\sin^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{3\pi}{12} + \dfrac{8\pi}{12} - \dfrac{2\pi}{12} = \dfrac{9\pi}{12} = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{5\pi}{4}\) (C) uses \(+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) for the last term. \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) (B) takes \(\cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\), confusing it with \(\sin^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2}\).
Key point: Find each principal value separately, then add.

questions.sub_topic: The relation "less than or equal to" on Z
questions.question: On \(\mathbb{Z}\), the relation \(R = \{(a, b) : a \le b\}\) is:
options: A) Reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
C) Symmetric and transitive but not reflexive
D) Reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
Why: \(a \le a\) (reflexive); \(a \le b\) and \(b \le c\) give \(a \le c\) (transitive); but \(1 \le 2\) while \(2 \not\le 1\) (not symmetric).
Why not the others: (B) claims symmetry. (C) denies reflexivity. (D) denies transitivity.
Key point: One counterexample is enough to disprove a property.

questions.sub_topic: Cartesian to vector form of a line
questions.question: The vector form of the line \(\dfrac{x - 5}{3} = \dfrac{y + 4}{7} = \dfrac{z - 6}{2}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\vec{r} = 5\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 6\hat{k} + \lambda(3\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} + 2\hat{k})\)
Given: point \((5, -4, 6)\), direction ratios \(3, 7, 2\)
Formula: \(\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}\)
Step 1: \(\vec{r} = 5\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 6\hat{k} + \lambda(3\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} + 2\hat{k})\)
Common mistake: (A) swaps the point and the direction. (B) reads \(y + 4\) as \(y_1 = 4\). (D) changes every sign of the point.
Key point: \(y + 4 = y - (-4)\), so \(y_1 = -4\).

questions.sub_topic: Standard integral 1/√(x² + a²)
questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2 + 4}}\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\log\left|x + \sqrt{x^2 + 4}\right| + C\)
Given: \(a = 2\)
Formula: \(\int \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2 + a^2}} = \log\left|x + \sqrt{x^2 + a^2}\right| + C\)
Step 1: \(\log\left|x + \sqrt{x^2 + 4}\right| + C\)
Common mistake: (A) is for \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}}\). (B) is for \(\dfrac{1}{x^2 + a^2}\), without the root.
Key point: Match the exact form: square root, and plus or minus.

questions.sub_topic: One red and one black with replacement
questions.question: A bag has 4 red and 6 black balls. Two balls are drawn one at a time with replacement. The probability that one is red and the other black is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(0.48\)
Given: \(P(R) = 0.4\), \(P(B) = 0.6\) on every draw
Formula: \(P = P(RB) + P(BR)\)
Step 1: \(0.4 \times 0.6 + 0.6 \times 0.4 = 0.24 + 0.24 = 0.48\)
Common mistake: \(0.24\) (A) counts only red first, then black.
Key point: "One of each" can happen in two orders.

questions.sub_topic: Where the modulus of x − 2 has a corner
questions.question: The function \(f(x) = |x - 2|\) is not differentiable at \(x =\):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(2\)
Given: \(f(x) = x - 2\) for \(x \ge 2\); \(f(x) = 2 - x\) for \(x < 2\)
Formula: compare the left and right derivatives at the joining point
Step 1: At \(x = 2\): left derivative \(-1\), right derivative \(+1\)
Step 2: They differ, so \(f\) is not differentiable at \(x = 2\)
Common mistake: \(0\) (A) thinks of \(|x|\), whose corner is at 0. \(-2\) (B) solves \(x + 2 = 0\).
Key point: \(|x - a|\) has its corner at \(x = a\).

questions.sub_topic: Implicit slope with an xy term
questions.question: For the curve \(x^2 + xy + y^2 = 7\), the value of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) at \((1, 2)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(-\dfrac{4}{5}\)
Given: \(x^2 + xy + y^2 = 7\)
Formula: differentiate with respect to \(x\), using the product rule on \(xy\)
Step 1: \(2x + y + x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2y\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{2x + y}{x + 2y}\)
Step 3: At \((1, 2)\): \(-\dfrac{4}{5}\)
Common mistake: \(-\dfrac{5}{4}\) (C) inverts the fraction. \(-1\) (D) forgets the product rule on \(xy\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(xy) = y + x\dfrac{dy}{dx}\).

questions.sub_topic: Orders of products of a 3 × 2 and a 2 × 3 matrix
questions.question:
\(A\) is of order \(3 \times 2\) and \(B\) is of order \(2 \times 3\). Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Order of \(AB\)
(B) Order of \(BA\)
(C) Order of \(A^T\)
(D) Number of entries in \(A\)

List-II
(I) \(2 \times 2\)
(II) \(6\)
(III) \(2 \times 3\)
(IV) \(3 \times 3\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(II)
Step 1: \((3 \times 2)(2 \times 3) = 3 \times 3\) (IV)
Step 2: \((2 \times 3)(3 \times 2) = 2 \times 2\) (I)
Step 3: \(A^T\) is \(2 \times 3\) (III)
Step 4: \(3 \times 2 = 6\) entries (II)
Common mistake: (A) swaps \(AB\) and \(BA\). (B) swaps \(BA\) and \(A^T\). (D) swaps \(A^T\) and the number of entries.
Key point: \(AB\) and \(BA\) can both exist and still have different orders.

questions.sub_topic: Scalar that makes a vector a unit vector
questions.question: \(\lambda(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})\) is a unit vector when \(\lambda\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\)
Given: \(|\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}| = \sqrt{3}\)
Formula: \(|\lambda\vec{a}| = |\lambda||\vec{a}| = 1\)
Step 1: \(|\lambda|\sqrt{3} = 1 \Rightarrow \lambda = \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\)
Common mistake: \(\pm\dfrac{1}{3}\) (A) divides by the sum of the components instead of the magnitude.
Key point: Divide by the magnitude, and remember both signs.

questions.sub_topic: Midpoint of a segment in space
questions.question: The position vector of the midpoint of the segment joining \(P(2, 3, 4)\) and \(Q(4, 1, -2)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}\)
Given: \(\vec{p} = (2, 3, 4)\), \(\vec{q} = (4, 1, -2)\)
Formula: midpoint \(= \dfrac{\vec{p} + \vec{q}}{2}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{(6, 4, 2)}{2} = (3, 2, 1)\)
Common mistake: (B) forgets to halve. (D) is \(\vec{q} - \vec{p}\).
Key point: Average the corresponding coordinates.

questions.sub_topic: Partial fractions with equal coefficients
questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x + 1}{x(x + 2)}\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\dfrac{1}{2}\log|x(x + 2)| + C\)
Given: \(\dfrac{x + 1}{x(x + 2)} = \dfrac{A}{x} + \dfrac{B}{x + 2}\), so \(x + 1 = A(x + 2) + Bx\)
Formula: substitute convenient values of \(x\)
Step 1: \(x = 0\): \(1 = 2A \Rightarrow A = \dfrac{1}{2}\); \(x = -2\): \(-1 = -2B \Rightarrow B = \dfrac{1}{2}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{1}{2}\log|x| + \dfrac{1}{2}\log|x + 2| = \dfrac{1}{2}\log|x(x + 2)| + C\)
Common mistake: (C) takes \(B = -\dfrac{1}{2}\). (B) forgets the factor \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).
Key point: Also note \(x + 1 = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2 + 2x)\), which gives the same answer.

questions.sub_topic: Shortest distance between intersecting lines
questions.question: The shortest distance between the lines \(\dfrac{x - 1}{2} = \dfrac{y - 2}{3} = \dfrac{z - 3}{4}\) and \(\dfrac{x - 4}{5} = \dfrac{y - 1}{2} = \dfrac{z}{1}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(0\)
Given: \(\vec{a}_1 = (1, 2, 3)\), \(\vec{b}_1 = (2, 3, 4)\); \(\vec{a}_2 = (4, 1, 0)\), \(\vec{b}_2 = (5, 2, 1)\)
Formula: \(d = \dfrac{|(\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2)\cdot(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)|}{|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2|}\)
Step 1: \(\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = (3 - 8)\hat{i} - (2 - 20)\hat{j} + (4 - 15)\hat{k} = (-5, 18, -11)\)
Step 2: \(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = (3, -1, -3)\); dot product \(= -15 - 18 + 33 = 0\)
Step 3: \(d = 0\), so the lines intersect
Common mistake: (D) puts \(|\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1|\)-type numbers in the numerator instead of the triple product.
Key point: A zero scalar triple product means the lines meet.

questions.sub_topic: Maxima of four objectives on one region
questions.question:
The corner points of a bounded feasible region are \((0, 0)\), \((6, 0)\), \((4, 3)\) and \((0, 5)\). Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Objective function)
(A) \(Z = x + y\)
(B) \(Z = 2x + y\)
(C) \(Z = x + 3y\)
(D) \(Z = 3x + 4y\)

List-II (Maximum value)
(I) \(7\)
(II) \(24\)
(III) \(12\)
(IV) \(15\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Step 1: \(x + y\): \(0, 6, 7, 5\) → 7 (I)
Step 2: \(2x + y\): \(0, 12, 11, 5\) → 12 (III)
Step 3: \(x + 3y\): \(0, 6, 13, 15\) → 15 (IV)
Step 4: \(3x + 4y\): \(0, 18, 24, 20\) → 24 (II)
Common mistake: (A) swaps the first two. (B) swaps \(2x + y\) and \(x + 3y\). (C) swaps the last two.
Key point: Tabulate every corner for every objective.

questions.sub_topic: A determinant with proportional rows
questions.question:
For \(\Delta = \begin{vmatrix}1&2&3\\2&4&6\\1&0&1\end{vmatrix}\), consider the following statements:
(A) \(\Delta = 0\).
(B) The corresponding matrix is singular.
(C) The cofactor \(A_{33} = 0\).
(D) The minor \(M_{11} = 6\).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) Row 2 is twice row 1. (B) follows from (A). (C) \(A_{33} = (+1)\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{vmatrix} = 4 - 4 = 0\).
Why not the others: (D) is false: \(M_{11} = \begin{vmatrix}4&6\\0&1\end{vmatrix} = 4\). Options (B) and (C) include (D); (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: Proportional rows make a determinant zero.

questions.sub_topic: Collinear points by a determinant
questions.question: The points \((2, -3)\), \((k, -1)\) and \((0, 4)\) are collinear. Then \(k\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\dfrac{10}{7}\)
Given: collinear points enclose zero area
Formula: \(\begin{vmatrix}2&-3&1\\k&-1&1\\0&4&1\end{vmatrix} = 0\)
Step 1: \(2(-1 - 4) + 3(k - 0) + 1(4k - 0) = -10 + 3k + 4k\)
Step 2: \(7k - 10 = 0 \Rightarrow k = \dfrac{10}{7}\)
Common mistake: \(-\dfrac{10}{7}\) (B) takes the second cofactor as \(-3k\). \(\dfrac{7}{10}\) (C) inverts the fraction.
Key point: Collinear means the triangle's area is zero.

questions.sub_topic: Sine of an expression with an inverse sine
questions.question: The value of \(\sin\left[\dfrac{\pi}{3} - \sin^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right]\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(1\)
Given: \(\sin^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}\)
Formula: evaluate the bracket first
Step 1: \(\dfrac{\pi}{3} - \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\)
Step 2: \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 1\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) (A) uses \(+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\), giving \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}\).
Key point: \(\sin^{-1}(-x) = -\sin^{-1}x\).

questions.sub_topic: Rate of change of the area of a square
questions.question: The rate of change of the area of a square with respect to its side, when the side is 6 cm, is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(12\) cm²/cm
Given: \(A = a^2\)
Formula: \(\dfrac{dA}{da} = 2a\)
Step 1: \(2 \times 6 = 12\)
Common mistake: \(36\) (A) is the area. \(24\) (B) is the perimeter.
Key point: Differentiate the area formula.

questions.sub_topic: Chain rule for cos(x³)
questions.question: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos(x^3)\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(-3x^2\sin(x^3)\)
Given: outer \(\cos u\), inner \(u = x^3\)
Formula: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos u = -\sin u\,\dfrac{du}{dx}\)
Step 1: \(-\sin(x^3) \cdot 3x^2\)
Common mistake: (A) forgets the inner derivative. (B) loses the minus sign.
Key point: The derivative of cosine is negative sine.

questions.sub_topic: Number of symmetric relations on two elements
questions.question: The number of symmetric relations on the set \(\{1, 2\}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(8\)
Given: pairs \((1,1), (2,2)\) and the pair-of-pairs \(\{(1,2), (2,1)\}\)
Formula: in a symmetric relation, \((1,2)\) and \((2,1)\) are both in or both out
Step 1: Free choices: \((1,1)\), \((2,2)\), and the pair together: 3 choices
Step 2: \(2^3 = 8\)
Common mistake: \(16\) (A) counts all relations.
Key point: Off-diagonal pairs come in matched couples.

questions.sub_topic: Linear equation with I.F. x²
questions.question: The solution of \(x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2y = x^2\) (\(x > 0\)) with \(y(1) = 1\) gives \(y(2)\) equal to:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\dfrac{19}{16}\)
Given: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \dfrac{2}{x}y = x\)
Formula: I.F. \(= e^{\int 2/x\,dx} = x^2\)
Step 1: \(yx^2 = \int x \cdot x^2 dx = \dfrac{x^4}{4} + C\), so \(y = \dfrac{x^2}{4} + \dfrac{C}{x^2}\)
Step 2: \(y(1) = 1\): \(\dfrac{1}{4} + C = 1 \Rightarrow C = \dfrac{3}{4}\)
Step 3: \(y(2) = 1 + \dfrac{3}{16} = \dfrac{19}{16}\)
Common mistake: \(1\) (A) drops the constant term. \(\dfrac{13}{16}\) (C) subtracts \(\dfrac{3}{16}\).
Key point: Divide by \(x\) first to get the standard form.

questions.sub_topic: Determinant of the inverse of a product
questions.question: For \(A = \begin{bmatrix}2&3\\1&-4\end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\-1&3\end{bmatrix}\), the value of \(|(AB)^{-1}|\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(-\dfrac{1}{11}\)
Given: \(|A| = -8 - 3 = -11\), \(|B| = 3 - 2 = 1\)
Formula: \(|AB| = |A||B|\), \(|M^{-1}| = \dfrac{1}{|M|}\)
Step 1: \(|AB| = -11\)
Step 2: \(|(AB)^{-1}| = -\dfrac{1}{11}\)
Common mistake: \(-11\) (A) stops at \(|AB|\). \(\dfrac{1}{11}\) (C) loses the sign of \(|A|\).
Key point: No need to multiply the matrices; use determinant rules.

questions.sub_topic: Neither of two independent events happens
questions.question: \(A\) and \(B\) are independent with \(P(A) = 0.5\) and \(P(B) = 0.4\). The probability that neither happens is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(0.3\)
Given: \(P(A') = 0.5\), \(P(B') = 0.6\)
Formula: \(A'\) and \(B'\) are independent too, so \(P(A' \cap B') = P(A')P(B')\)
Step 1: \(0.5 \times 0.6 = 0.3\)
Common mistake: \(0.2\) (B) is \(P(A \cap B)\). \(0.7\) (D) is \(P(A \cup B)\).
Key point: "Neither" is the complement of "at least one".

questions.sub_topic: A function on N that halves and rounds up
questions.question: \(f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\) is defined by \(f(n) = \dfrac{n + 1}{2}\) if \(n\) is odd and \(f(n) = \dfrac{n}{2}\) if \(n\) is even. Then \(f\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Onto but not one-one
Why: \(f(1) = 1 = f(2)\), so \(f\) is not one-one. Every \(m \in \mathbb{N}\) equals \(f(2m)\), so \(f\) is onto.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) claim one-one, which \(f(1) = f(2)\) disproves. (D) misses that every \(m\) is reached.
Key point: For onto, produce a pre-image for every element of the codomain.

questions.sub_topic: A second-order identity for eˣ sin x
questions.question: If \(y = e^x\sin x\), then \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} - 2\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2y\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(0\)
Given: \(y = e^x\sin x\)
Formula: product rule twice
Step 1: \(y' = e^x\sin x + e^x\cos x = e^x(\sin x + \cos x)\)
Step 2: \(y'' = e^x(\sin x + \cos x) + e^x(\cos x - \sin x) = 2e^x\cos x\)
Step 3: \(2e^x\cos x - 2e^x(\sin x + \cos x) + 2e^x\sin x = 0\)
Common mistake: \(2e^x\cos x\) (A) stops at \(y''\).
Key point: Write every derivative in terms of \(e^x\sin x\) and \(e^x\cos x\), then collect.

questions.sub_topic: Homogeneous equation (x² + y²)/(xy)
questions.question: The general solution of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x^2 + y^2}{xy}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(y^2 = 2x^2\log|x| + Cx^2\)
Given: put \(y = vx\): \(v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{1 + v^2}{v} = \dfrac{1}{v} + v\)
Formula: separate \(v\) and \(x\)
Step 1: \(x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{v} \Rightarrow v\,dv = \dfrac{dx}{x}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{v^2}{2} = \log|x| + c \Rightarrow \dfrac{y^2}{x^2} = 2\log|x| + C\)
Step 3: \(y^2 = 2x^2\log|x| + Cx^2\)
Common mistake: (A) forgets the factor 2 from \(\dfrac{v^2}{2}\). (D) forgets to replace \(v\) by \(\dfrac{y}{x}\).
Key point: Substitute back \(v = \dfrac{y}{x}\) at the end.

questions.sub_topic: Number of five-yearly moving averages
questions.question: For data covering 10 years, the number of five-yearly moving averages that can be computed is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(6\)
Given: \(N = 10\), period \(k = 5\)
Formula: number of moving averages \(= N - k + 1\)
Step 1: \(10 - 5 + 1 = 6\)
Common mistake: \(5\) (B) uses \(N - k\). \(8\) (D) loses only one value at each end.
Key point: A \(k\)-period average loses \(k - 1\) values in all.

questions.sub_topic: Value of a bond priced at a discount
questions.question: A bond of face value ₹1,000 pays an 8% annual coupon and is redeemed at par after 2 years. If the market yield is 10% per annum, its value is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹965.29
Given: coupon ₹80 per year, redemption ₹1,000, \(i = 0.10\)
Formula: value \(= \dfrac{C}{1 + i} + \dfrac{C + F}{(1 + i)^2}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{80}{1.1} \approx 72.73\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{1080}{1.21} \approx 892.56\)
Step 3: Value \(\approx 965.29\)
Common mistake: ₹1,000 (A) is the par value. ₹1,035.67 (B) is the value when the yield is below the coupon rate.
Key point: When the yield exceeds the coupon rate, the bond sells at a discount.

questions.sub_topic: Where log x − x increases
questions.question: The function \(f(x) = \log x - x\) (\(x > 0\)) is strictly increasing on:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \((0, 1)\)
Given: \(f'(x) = \dfrac{1}{x} - 1 = \dfrac{1 - x}{x}\)
Formula: increasing where \(f'(x) > 0\)
Step 1: For \(x > 0\), \(f'(x) > 0 \iff x < 1\), so \(0 < x < 1\)
Common mistake: (A) is where \(f\) decreases. (D) ignores the domain \(x > 0\).
Key point: Respect the domain of \(\log x\).

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.sub_topic: A double inequality
questions.question: The solution set of \(2 \le 3x - 4 \le 11\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(2 \le x \le 5\)
Given: \(2 \le 3x - 4 \le 11\)
Formula: do the same operation on all three parts
Step 1: Add 4: \(6 \le 3x \le 15\)
Step 2: Divide by 3: \(2 \le x \le 5\)
Common mistake: (D) stops before dividing by 3. (A) drops the equality signs.
Key point: "\(\le\)" keeps the end points.

questions.sub_topic: Mean of a small sample
questions.question: The mean of the sample 12, 15, 18, 15 is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(15\)
Given: \(n = 4\), \(\sum x = 60\)
Formula: \(\bar{x} = \dfrac{\sum x}{n}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{60}{4} = 15\)
Common mistake: \(60\) (C) is the total, not the mean.
Key point: Divide the total by the number of values.

questions.sub_topic: CAGR over three years
questions.question: An investment of ₹8,000 grows to ₹10,648 in 3 years. Its compound annual growth rate is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(10\%\)
Given: initial ₹8,000, final ₹10,648, \(n = 3\)
Formula: CAGR \(= \left(\dfrac{\text{final}}{\text{initial}}\right)^{1/n} - 1\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{10{,}648}{8{,}000} = 1.331\)
Step 2: \((1.331)^{1/3} = 1.1\), so CAGR \(= 10\%\)
Common mistake: \(11\%\) (A) divides the total growth of 33.1% by 3. \(33.1\%\) (D) is the total growth.
Key point: CAGR is a compound, not simple, average.

questions.sub_topic: Values of k making a matrix singular
questions.question: The matrix \(\begin{bmatrix}k&2\\3&k - 1\end{bmatrix}\) is singular when \(k\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(3\) or \(-2\)
Given: singular means determinant zero
Formula: \(k(k - 1) - 6 = 0\)
Step 1: \(k^2 - k - 6 = 0 \Rightarrow (k - 3)(k + 2) = 0\)
Step 2: \(k = 3\) or \(k = -2\)
Common mistake: (B) gets the signs of the factors wrong. (D) keeps only one root.
Key point: A quadratic condition can give two values.

questions.sub_topic: Revenue from a linear demand — which claims fail
questions.question:
The demand function is \(p = 40 - 2x\). Consider the following statements:
(A) The revenue function is \(R(x) = 40x - 2x^2\).
(B) Marginal revenue is \(40 - 4x\).
(C) Revenue is greatest at \(x = 20\).
(D) The greatest revenue is 200.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false: \(MR = 40 - 4x = 0\) at \(x = 10\); at \(x = 20\) the price, and so the revenue, is zero.
Why not the others: (A) \(R = px\). (B) \(R'(x) = 40 - 4x\). (D) \(R(10) = 400 - 200 = 200\). Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Revenue is greatest where marginal revenue is zero.

questions.sub_topic: Second derivative of a quartic at a point
questions.question: If \(y = x^4 - 2x^2\), then \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) at \(x = 1\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(8\)
Given: \(y = x^4 - 2x^2\)
Formula: differentiate twice
Step 1: \(y' = 4x^3 - 4x\)
Step 2: \(y'' = 12x^2 - 4\); at \(x = 1\): \(8\)
Common mistake: \(0\) (B) is \(y'\) at \(x = 1\). \(-1\) (D) is \(y\) at \(x = 1\).
Key point: Differentiate fully before substituting.

questions.sub_topic: Decision in a one-sample t-test
questions.question: A sample of 16 has mean 53 and standard deviation 4 (divisor \(n - 1\)). \(H_0: \mu = 50\) is tested at the 5% level; the two-tailed table value of \(t\) for 15 degrees of freedom is 2.13. The result is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(t = 3\); reject \(H_0\)
Given: \(n = 16\), \(\bar{x} = 53\), \(s = 4\), \(\mu = 50\)
Formula: \(t = \dfrac{\bar{x} - \mu}{s/\sqrt{n}}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \dfrac{4}{4} = 1\), so \(t = 3\)
Step 2: \(|t| = 3 > 2.13\), so \(H_0\) is rejected
Common mistake: (B) reverses the decision rule. (C) divides by \(s\) instead of \(s/\sqrt{n}\). (D) multiplies by \(\sqrt{n}\) twice.
Key point: Reject \(H_0\) when \(|t|\) exceeds the table value.

questions.sub_topic: A scalar times a matrix
questions.question: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\0&4\end{bmatrix}\), then \(3A\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\begin{bmatrix}3&-6\\0&12\end{bmatrix}\)
Given: \(k = 3\)
Formula: multiply every entry by \(k\)
Step 1: \(\begin{bmatrix}3&-6\\0&12\end{bmatrix}\)
Common mistake: (A) multiplies only the first entry. (B) adds 3 to every entry.
Key point: Scalar multiplication affects every entry.

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.sub_topic: A negative number modulo 5
questions.question: The value of \(-17 \bmod 5\) (the remainder from \(\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}\)) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(3\)
Given: write \(-17 = 5q + r\) with \(0 \le r < 5\)
Step 1: \(-17 = 5(-4) + 3\)
Step 2: \(r = 3\)
Common mistake: \(-2\) (A) is not in the allowed range. \(2\) (B) takes \(17 \bmod 5\) and keeps it.
Key point: The remainder must be non-negative.

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.sub_topic: By how much A beats B over 400 m
questions.question: A runs 400 m in 80 s and B runs it in 90 s. By about how many metres does A beat B?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(44.4\) m
Given: B's speed \(= \dfrac{400}{90}\) m/s
Formula: distance B covers in A's time
Step 1: In 80 s, B runs \(\dfrac{400}{90} \times 80 = \dfrac{3200}{9} \approx 355.6\) m
Step 2: A wins by \(400 - 355.6 \approx 44.4\) m
Common mistake: \(10\) m (C) gives the time difference in seconds. \(50\) m (A) uses A's speed for the last 10 s.
Key point: Find where the loser is when the winner finishes.

questions.sub_topic: Producer surplus with a quadratic supply
questions.question: The supply function is \(p = 4 + x^2\) and the market price is ₹13. The producer surplus is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹18
Given: \(13 = 4 + x_0^2 \Rightarrow x_0 = 3\)
Formula: PS \(= p_0x_0 - \int_0^{x_0}S(x)\,dx\)
Step 1: \(p_0x_0 = 13 \times 3 = 39\)
Step 2: \(\int_0^3(4 + x^2)dx = 12 + 9 = 21\)
Step 3: PS \(= 39 - 21 = 18\)
Common mistake: ₹21 (A) is the area under the supply curve. ₹39 (B) is total revenue.
Key point: Producer surplus lies between the price line and the supply curve.

questions.sub_topic: E(X²) from the mean and variance
questions.question: A random variable has \(E(X) = 3\) and \(\text{Var}(X) = 4\). Then \(E(X^2)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(13\)
Given: \(E(X) = 3\), \(\text{Var}(X) = 4\)
Formula: \(\text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2\)
Step 1: \(E(X^2) = 4 + 9 = 13\)
Common mistake: \(7\) (A) adds 3 instead of 9. \(5\) (C) subtracts.
Key point: Rearrange the variance formula.

questions.sub_topic: n of a binomial from its mean and variance
questions.question: A binomial distribution has mean 4 and variance 3. The number of trials \(n\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(16\)
Given: \(np = 4\), \(npq = 3\)
Formula: divide to find \(q\)
Step 1: \(q = \dfrac{3}{4}\), so \(p = \dfrac{1}{4}\)
Step 2: \(n = \dfrac{4}{1/4} = 16\)
Common mistake: \(12\) (A) uses \(nq = 4\). \(\dfrac{64}{3}\) (D) computes \(\dfrac{4}{p \cdot q} = \dfrac{4}{3/16}\), dividing by \(q\) as well.
Key point: \(q = \dfrac{\text{variance}}{\text{mean}}\).

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.sub_topic: Four quantities for a boat in a stream
questions.question:
A boat's speed in still water is 10 km/h and the stream flows at 2 km/h. Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Speed downstream
(B) Speed upstream
(C) Time to go 24 km downstream
(D) Time to go 24 km upstream

List-II
(I) \(3\) h
(II) \(12\) km/h
(III) \(8\) km/h
(IV) \(2\) h
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Step 1: Downstream \(= 10 + 2 = 12\) km/h (II)
Step 2: Upstream \(= 10 - 2 = 8\) km/h (III)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{24}{12} = 2\) h (IV)
Step 4: \(\dfrac{24}{8} = 3\) h (I)
Common mistake: (B) swaps the two speeds. (C) swaps the two times. (D) mixes a speed with a time.
Key point: Downstream is faster, so it takes less time.

questions.sub_topic: Definite integral of (x + 1)²
questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int_0^1(x + 1)^2\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\dfrac{7}{3}\)
Given: antiderivative \(\dfrac{(x + 1)^3}{3}\)
Formula: \(F(1) - F(0)\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{8}{3} - \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{7}{3}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{8}{3}\) (B) forgets that \(F(0) = \dfrac{1}{3}\), not 0.
Key point: The lower limit does not always give zero.

questions.sub_topic: Writing the constraints of a production problem
questions.question:
A firm makes \(x\) tables and \(y\) chairs. A table needs 3 hours and a chair 2 hours of labour; 60 hours are available, and at least 5 tables must be made. Consider the following statements:
(A) The labour constraint is \(3x + 2y \le 60\).
(B) The order constraint is \(x \ge 5\).
(C) The non-negativity constraints are \(x, y \ge 0\).
(D) The labour constraint is \(3x + 2y \ge 60\).
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D) only
Why: Only (D) is false: labour used cannot exceed the 60 hours available, so the sign is \(\le\).
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) translate the conditions correctly. Options (A), (B) and (C) name a true statement as false.
Key point: "Available" gives \(\le\); "at least" gives \(\ge\).

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.sub_topic: Milk left after two replacements
questions.question: A container holds 40 litres of milk. 4 litres are removed and replaced with water, and the process is repeated once more. The milk now in the container is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(32.4\) litres
Given: initial 40 L, 4 L replaced each time, 2 times
Formula: milk left \(= 40\left(1 - \dfrac{4}{40}\right)^2\)
Step 1: \(1 - \dfrac{4}{40} = 0.9\)
Step 2: \(40 \times 0.81 = 32.4\) L
Common mistake: \(32\) L (B) subtracts 4 L of milk twice, but the second removal takes out some water too.
Key point: Each replacement keeps the same fraction of the remaining milk.

questions.sub_topic: A negative standard normal variate
questions.question: \(X\) is normal with mean 100 and standard deviation 15. The standard normal variate for \(X = 85\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(-1\)
Given: \(\mu = 100\), \(\sigma = 15\), \(X = 85\)
Formula: \(Z = \dfrac{X - \mu}{\sigma}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{85 - 100}{15} = -1\)
Common mistake: \(1\) (B) loses the sign. \(-15\) (C) forgets to divide by \(\sigma\).
Key point: Values below the mean have negative \(Z\).

questions.sub_topic: Terms of financial mathematics
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Sinking fund
(B) Perpetuity
(C) Coupon rate
(D) EMI

List-II
(I) Payments that continue forever
(II) Interest rate paid on a bond's face value
(III) Periodic deposits made to meet a future liability
(IV) Equal monthly payment covering interest and principal
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(IV)
Why: A sinking fund accumulates deposits for a future need (III); a perpetuity never ends (I); the coupon rate is paid on face value (II); an EMI repays a loan in equal instalments (IV).
Why not the others: (B) swaps the sinking fund and the perpetuity. (C) swaps the perpetuity and the coupon rate. (D) swaps the coupon rate and the EMI.
Key point: A sinking fund saves up; an EMI pays back.

questions.sub_topic: Integral of e^(2x) + 1/(x + 1)
questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int\left(e^{2x} + \dfrac{1}{x + 1}\right)dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{1}{2}e^{2x} + \log|x + 1| + C\)
Given: integrate term by term
Formula: \(\int e^{ax}dx = \dfrac{1}{a}e^{ax}\); \(\int \dfrac{dx}{x + 1} = \log|x + 1|\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1}{2}e^{2x} + \log|x + 1| + C\)
Common mistake: (A) multiplies by 2 instead of dividing. (B) differentiates the second term.
Key point: Divide by the coefficient of \(x\) in the exponent.

questions.sub_topic: Standard deviation of a Poisson distribution
questions.question: A Poisson distribution has mean 4. Its standard deviation is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(2\)
Given: \(\lambda = 4\)
Formula: variance \(= \lambda\), SD \(= \sqrt{\lambda}\)
Step 1: \(\sqrt{4} = 2\)
Common mistake: \(4\) (A) is the variance. \(16\) (B) squares the mean.
Key point: SD is the square root of the variance.

questions.sub_topic: Maximum at the intersection of two constraints
questions.question: The maximum value of \(Z = 4x + 3y\) subject to \(2x + y \le 10\), \(x + 3y \le 15\), \(x, y \ge 0\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(24\)
Given: constraints \(2x + y \le 10\), \(x + 3y \le 15\)
Formula: evaluate \(Z\) at the corners
Step 1: Intersection: \(y = 10 - 2x\); \(x + 30 - 6x = 15 \Rightarrow x = 3\), \(y = 4\)
Step 2: Corners \((0, 0)\), \((5, 0)\), \((3, 4)\), \((0, 5)\) give \(Z = 0, 20, 24, 15\)
Step 3: Maximum \(Z = 24\)
Common mistake: \(30\) (D) uses \((0, 10)\), which breaks \(x + 3y \le 15\). \(20\) (A) misses the intersection corner.
Key point: Solve the two binding constraints together to find the inner corner.

questions.sub_topic: Binomial probability of at least five out of six
questions.question: For a binomial distribution with \(n = 6\) and \(p = \dfrac{1}{2}\), \(P(X \ge 5)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{7}{64}\)
Given: \(n = 6\), \(p = q = \dfrac{1}{2}\)
Formula: \(P(X \ge 5) = P(5) + P(6) = \dfrac{\binom{6}{5} + \binom{6}{6}}{2^6}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{6 + 1}{64} = \dfrac{7}{64}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{6}{64}\) (A) is \(P(X = 5)\) only. \(\dfrac{57}{64}\) (D) is \(P(X \le 4)\).
Key point: "At least 5" includes 5 and 6.

questions.sub_topic: Samples, statistics and the central limit theorem
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The standard error of the mean decreases as the sample size increases.
(B) For large samples, the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal.
(C) The value of a statistic varies from sample to sample.
(D) A parameter is calculated from a sample.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) SE \(= \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\). (B) is the central limit theorem. (C) different samples give different statistics.
Why not the others: (D) is false: a parameter describes the population; a statistic is calculated from a sample. Options (B) and (D) include (D); (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: Parameter–population, statistic–sample.

questions.sub_topic: Average cost at a given output
questions.question: For \(C(x) = 2x^2 + 3x + 75\), the average cost at \(x = 5\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(28\)
Given: \(C(5) = 50 + 15 + 75 = 140\)
Formula: \(AC = \dfrac{C(x)}{x}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{140}{5} = 28\)
Common mistake: \(140\) (A) is the total cost. \(23\) (B) is the marginal cost \(4x + 3\) at \(x = 5\).
Key point: Average cost divides total cost by output; marginal cost differentiates it.

questions.sub_topic: Half-yearly sinking fund for one year
questions.question: ₹5,000 is deposited at the end of every half-year for 1 year, earning 8% per annum compounded half-yearly. The amount at the end of the year is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹10,200
Given: \(R = 5{,}000\), \(i = 0.04\) per half-year, \(n = 2\)
Formula: \(A = R\left[\dfrac{(1 + i)^n - 1}{i}\right]\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{(1.04)^2 - 1}{0.04} = \dfrac{0.0816}{0.04} = 2.04\)
Step 2: \(A = 5{,}000 \times 2.04 = 10{,}200\)
Common mistake: ₹10,400 (B) gives interest to both deposits. ₹10,000 (A) gives none.
Key point: The last deposit earns no interest.

questions.sub_topic: Separable equation eˣ/y
questions.question: The general solution of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{e^x}{y}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(y^2 = 2e^x + C\)
Given: \(y\,dy = e^x\,dx\)
Formula: integrate both sides
Step 1: \(\dfrac{y^2}{2} = e^x + c\)
Step 2: \(y^2 = 2e^x + C\)
Common mistake: (C) forgets to double \(e^x\) when clearing the \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). (D) integrates \(y\,dy\) as \(\log y\).
Key point: Multiply every term by 2.

questions.sub_topic: Tenth power of an upper triangular matrix
questions.question: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\), then \(A^{10}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\begin{bmatrix}1&10\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\)
Given: \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\)
Formula: find the pattern in \(A^2, A^3\)
Step 1: \(A^2 = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\), \(A^3 = \begin{bmatrix}1&3\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\)
Step 2: So \(A^n = \begin{bmatrix}1&n\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\), and \(A^{10} = \begin{bmatrix}1&10\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\)
Common mistake: (C) multiplies every entry by 10. (D) puts the 10 below the diagonal.
Key point: Compute a few powers and look for the pattern.

questions.sub_topic: Trend value from two earlier trend values
questions.question: A straight-line trend gives trend values of 30 for 2019 and 36 for 2023. The trend value for 2026 is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(40.5\)
Given: change of 6 over 4 years
Formula: slope \(= \dfrac{36 - 30}{2023 - 2019} = 1.5\) per year
Step 1: From 2023 to 2026 is 3 years: \(36 + 3 \times 1.5 = 40.5\)
Common mistake: \(42\) (D) adds the whole 4-year change of 6. \(39\) (A) uses 1 per year.
Key point: A straight-line trend changes by the same amount every year.

questions.sub_topic: Pieces of a least squares trend line
questions.question:
For 5 years coded \(x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2\), the data give \(\sum y = 50\), \(\sum xy = 20\) and \(\sum x^2 = 10\). Match List-I with List-II for the trend line \(y = a + bx\).

List-I
(A) \(a\)
(B) \(b\)
(C) Trend value at \(x = 1\)
(D) Trend value at \(x = -2\)

List-II
(I) \(12\)
(II) \(6\)
(III) \(2\)
(IV) \(10\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Given: \(n = 5\), \(\sum x = 0\)
Step 1: \(a = \dfrac{50}{5} = 10\) (IV)
Step 2: \(b = \dfrac{20}{10} = 2\) (III)
Step 3: At \(x = 1\): \(10 + 2 = 12\) (I)
Step 4: At \(x = -2\): \(10 - 4 = 6\) (II)
Common mistake: (A) swaps \(a\) and \(b\). (B) swaps \(b\) and the value at \(x = 1\). (C) swaps the two trend values.
Key point: With \(\sum x = 0\), \(a\) is simply the mean of \(y\).

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.sub_topic: Last digit of a power of 3
questions.question: The last digit of \(3^{25}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(3\)
Given: last digits of \(3^1, 3^2, 3^3, 3^4\) are \(3, 9, 7, 1\), then they repeat
Formula: the last digit of \(3^n\) depends on \(n \bmod 4\)
Step 1: \(25 = 6 \times 4 + 1\), so \(25 \equiv 1 \pmod 4\)
Step 2: Last digit \(= 3\)
Common mistake: \(1\) (D) assumes a multiple of 4. \(7\) (C) uses remainder 3.
Key point: The last digit is the remainder modulo 10, which cycles every 4 powers for 3.

questions.sub_topic: Facts about two particular matrices
questions.question:
For \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\), consider the following statements:
(A) \(AB \ne BA\).
(B) \(B^2 = I\).
(C) \(|AB| = 2\).
(D) \(A\) is singular.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) \(AB = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\4&3\end{bmatrix}\), \(BA = \begin{bmatrix}3&4\\1&2\end{bmatrix}\). (B) swapping rows twice gives \(I\). (C) \(|A||B| = (-2)(-1) = 2\).
Why not the others: (D) is false: \(|A| = -2 \ne 0\). Options (B) and (D) include (D); (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: Multiplying by \(B\) on the left swaps rows; on the right, it swaps columns.
